summary: Computing constrained traffic engineering paths across multiple domains is a key requirement. This experimental RFC defines domain subobjects for PCEP, letting a domain such as an IGP area or autonomous system be named in path computation.

eli5.summary: Telling a route planner to go through or avoid certain regions of the network, not only particular routers.

questions: what is a pcep domain sequence
how to exclude an as in pcep
what is the pcep iro and xro
subtitle: New route-object elements that let path computation name whole domains, such as IGP areas and autonomous systems, to cross or avoid.

tldr.problem: Computing constrained paths across several domains assumes that the sequence of domains to cross is already known, and PCEP had no way to express a 4-byte AS number or an IGP area in its route objects.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three subobjects: a 4-byte AS number (type 5), an OSPF Area ID (type 6) and an IS-IS Area ID (type 7). They are used in the IRO, XRO, EXRS and ERO to write down a domain sequence.
tldr.outcome: A PCC or PCE can say which domains a path must cross or avoid. It is an Experimental protocol, and legacy PCEs treat the new subobjects as a malformed object.

facts.label: IS-IS Area ID subobject
facts.value: Type 7, length at least 8 and a multiple of 4

today: RFC 7897 is an Experimental RFC, and no RFC in its metadata obsoletes or updates it. It is the PCEP companion to RFC 7898 for RSVP-TE, and it says it could move to the Standards Track once implementation and deployment results are available.

sections.title: Why Domains Need Names in PCEP
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) can compute end-to-end paths across multiple domains, using per-domain computation (RFC 5152) or Backward-Recursive PCE-Based Computation (RFC 5441). Both assume that the sequence of domains from source to destination is already known, either fixed by the operator or found by other means. The same is true for point-to-multipoint trees in RFC 7334.

PCEP already had the Include Route Object (IRO) and Explicit Route Object (ERO) from RFC 5440, and the Exclude Route Object (XRO) and Explicit Exclusion Route subobject (EXRS) from RFC 5521. RFC 3209 allows an AS as an abstract node, but only with a 2-byte AS number. This document adds subobjects for 4-byte AS numbers (RFC 6793) and IGP areas.

It is a companion to the RSVP-TE extensions in RFC 7898, and its procedures are Experimental. The experiment is intended to end two years after publication.
sections.eli5: Route planners knew how to say 'go through this exact router' but not 'go through this whole region'. This RFC adds a way to name whole regions.

sections.title: Domains and Domain Sequences
sections.content:
A domain is any collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computational responsibility. Examples are an IGP area and an Autonomous System (AS). A domain can be uniquely identified by an area ID, an AS number, or both.

A domain sequence is an ordered sequence of domains traversed to reach the destination domain. It can be a constraint in a path computation request, or the result of a computation, for example when a parent PCE in a hierarchical PCE (RFC 6805) returns it in a reply. For a P2P path the domains appear in the order crossed; for a P2MP path the domain tree is a list of domain sequences.

A sequence can be made of AS numbers, area IDs, boundary node IDs and inter-AS link addresses. A PCE can use it to select the next PCE in collaborative computation, to constrain which domains are used or excluded, or to identify the next domain in per-domain computation. The mapping from domains to responsible PCEs is not defined in this document.
sections.eli5: A domain is a region of the network run by one team. A domain sequence is the list of regions your trip passes through, in order, like countries on a journey.

sections.title: The New Subobjects
sections.content:
Three subobject types are defined, with the same values in the IRO and the XRO, and identical subobjects carried in RSVP-TE by RFC 7898.

  • Type 5, 4-byte AS number. Length is 8. The AS Number field is 4 bytes; a 2-byte AS number uses the low-order bits 16 through 31, with the high-order bits set to zero.
  • Type 6, OSPF Area ID. Length is 8, and the Area ID is a 4-byte number.
  • Type 7, IS-IS Area ID. The length is variable, MUST be at least 8 and MUST be a multiple of 4. An Area-Len field gives the real identifier length in octets, from 1 to 13, and the area ID is padded with trailing zeroes to a 4-byte boundary.

The first bit is the L bit in an IRO (defined in RFC 3209, with its IRO use set out in RFC 7896) and the X bit in an XRO. Reserved bits are zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. In an XRO, X set to 0 means the domain MUST be excluded; X set to 1 means it SHOULD be avoided but MAY be included subject to PCE policy and the absence of a viable path.
sections.eli5: There are three new kinds of label: one for a big-number network ID, one for an OSPF area, and one for an IS-IS area. Each says 'this region' in its own style.

sections.title: Using Domain Subobjects in Objects
sections.content:
In an IRO, the new subobjects can be mixed with existing IPv4, IPv6 and unnumbered interface subobjects. The IRO is treated as an ordered list, per RFC 7896. A PCE reads it while tracking a current AS and a current area. The current AS starts as the PCC's AS, an AS subobject changes it, an area subobject is assumed to belong to the current AS, and a globally routable IP address moves it to the AS that owns that address. When the current AS changes, the current area is reset. If the PCE is not responsible for the current AS or area, it picks the next PCE from the domain sequence.

A PCE that does not recognize the new subobjects responds as for a malformed object (RFC 5440). It MAY include the IRO in the PCErr message. In a reply, a PCE MAY supply the IRO along with the NO-PATH object. A PCC is advised to use AS and area subobjects when building the sequence.

In an XRO, the same subobjects exclude domains. IGP area subobjects in an XRO are local to the current AS, so to exclude an area in a different AS, the area subobject should go in an EXRS in the IRO. An EXRS limits the exclusion to the single hop between neighbouring IRO elements and does not change the current AS or area. In an ERO, the subobjects name abstract nodes, so a path can be an explicit sequence of domains, for example a parent PCE reply in H-PCE.
sections.eli5: The planner keeps track of which region it is in as it reads the list, and each region sign tells it you moved. If the planner does not know the new signs, it says the request is broken.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The extensions do not substantially change PCEP, so the security considerations of RFC 5440 apply unchanged. However, the new subobjects give finer control over the computed path. If a PCEP message is intercepted, modified or spoofed, an attacker could steer the path or make computation impossible. Implementations should therefore follow the RFC 5440 security mechanisms, including TCP security techniques, message authentication and protection against TCP denial of service. The RFC also notes that domain sequences can help an operator route around vulnerable parts of the network.

For manageability, the behaviour for including and excluding domains MUST be available for examination and MAY be configurable. Because no capabilities exchange tells a node whether a peer understands the new subobjects, manual configuration is needed to identify which PCEP peers take part in the experiment.
sections.eli5: Because the new labels give more control over the route, a trickster who fakes a message could do more harm. So the usual locks on the messages matter even more.
